utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, 27th of January, 2009. Good afternoon to the accused, first, to the Defence counsel, the witness, and the OTP representatives, and good afternoon to all the people assisting us. Before I give you the floor, Mr. Bos, for your last 15 minutes, let me return to what Ms. Alaburic said yesterday. I checked the transcript, the French transcript page 32003. There's no doubt, ambiguity at all. When I put the question, I put it as a question, with a question mark, saying this: "Mr. Petkovic [as interpreted], is it Mr. Petkovic who decided over ..." et cetera. So I made sure that I put the question as a question, not at all as a statement, as shown by the English translation. So in the future, in order to avoid this kind of problem, if you have any doubt as to what somebody said, wait until you have checked in the three languages, what was said, to avoid any waste of time, to cast doubts on people who have nothing to do with the problem at hand. You can imagine that I was not going to make a mistake that a first-year law student would make by drawing conclusions on the basis of a document that, in itself, raises a lot of issues. Furthermore, I noted at the end of the hearing that Ms. Alaburic had withdrawn what she had said originally, and I did take note of that, but I wanted to check what I had said exactly in the French transcript. That seemed to be so -- such a blunder that I had to check. It was done. I wanted to reassure you the question was indeed put as a question, with a question mark. So maybe during redirect, Mr. Stojic's Defence might return to the issue. Yes, Mr. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, greetings to everyone in the courtroom. I wish to thank you once again for your effort to clear up this sentence, which really sounded strange in the English language. I accepted already, without any reservations yesterday, your explanation that this was a hypothetical statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. The legal officer said that it was page 35927, whilst I have on my document "Page 32003." But we have already accumulated 35.000 pages, which is quite a huge number. Mr. Bos, you may proceed for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Marijan. In the remaining 15 minutes, I would like to take you back to the conclusions of your report, and I'll ask you to go to your report, to the section "Conclusions." Now, sir, one of my impressions after having read your full report, was that a number of your conclusions at the end of your report didn't really follow logically from what actually was discussed in the report, and let me give you an example of this and which is paragraph 129 of your report, one of the conclusions. There, you state: "During the entire period, whenever he was able to do it, Bruno Stojic was cooperative towards international organisations that were active at the territory of the HZ-HB." Now, first of all, what does Bruno Stojic's attitude towards international organisations have to do with the subject of your report, which concerns the structure of the HVO Defence Department? And, secondly, where in your report do you actually refer to this evidence showing that Bruno Stojic was cooperative to international organisations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, good afternoon, first of all, to everyone. I can't remember exactly the point in which I refer to Mr. Stojic's efforts, but the topic of my expert report is the Defence Department and Mr. Stojic; therefore, his position as head of the Defence Department, and I felt that this was an important question. And in the course of my studies, I saw a large number of documents. I didn't see any document that would be contrary to this. I think that he was indeed cooperative in his relations with international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, sir, you say that you can't exactly point to the -- you know, where in the report you refer to these efforts, but I put it to you that you don't refer at all in your report to these efforts, except in your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but I don't see what is being contested in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, what's being contested is that if you draft a report and you come to the conclusions, normally the conclusions would conclude what's been discussed in the reports, and clearly here, on this particular issue, you don't draw a conclusion on what's based in the report. You actually draw a conclusion and -- yeah, the conclusion, in fact, comes out of the blue. It doesn't support anything which is written in the report. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I couldn't agree with that, because in paragraph 294, I listed -- in my footnote, I listed all the documents on which I drew this conclusion. So it's not out of the blue. My entire report is based on documents. I think there's not a single secondary source, if my memory's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Marijan, you actually put it in the footnote, but what I am stating is that if you draw a conclusion, it should be a conclusion based on what you have written in the report and not just the footnote to the conclusion. But, anyway, we'll leave that point aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my friend's moving on, but of course questions should not be argumentative. They must be very specific questions. Perhaps my friend could, if he wishes to pursue this --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, I think we can move on, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you now to move to your first conclusion, which is under paragraph 126, and let me read out this conclusion to you: "The Croatian Community or Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna arose in the final phases of the collapse of Yugoslavia and the internal crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The crisis of the system and the continued warfare marked the activities of the HZ-HB, which was the local response to the collapse of central authority and the impossibility of an agreement with the other two peoples concerning the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Sir, I have a couple of questions on this particular conclusion. What sort of agreement were you referring to in that last sentence of your conclusion, and what was the objective of the Bosnian Croats as regard to the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Could you elaborate on this, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm originally -- misunderstood you. Oh, I see now, I see now what you are asking me. The fundamental issue, or at least my opinion, working on this, was closer to my original finding seven years ago, and analysing the documents that were available to me, that I managed to get hold of, my opinion and conclusion is that representatives of the authorities of Herceg-Bosna tried to come into agreement just before the war and during the war, and that such an agreement was never achieved because of different territorial aspirations of all three peoples. Each of the peoples had their own views of the war, their own tactics, and which actually led to the discord and the war. Now, you have asked the question of the aims. I think the aims of the Croats of Herceg-Bosna was an entity within Bosnia-Herzegovina. After all, one must always bear in mind that there was also the international aspect of this problem which favoured cantonalisation or provinces, but in any event, a certain delineation within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, in your answer you referred to your findings seven years ago. Were you actually referring to your evidence that you gave at that time in the Naletilic/Martinovic case and the expert report that you submitted in that particular case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am referring to those findings. I think at the time I provided a clearer answer, because I went into Croatian-Muslim problems and I focused on the relationship between the Croats and the Muslims, and in that report the Serbs were given relatively little space.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The last thing I would like to do now is put a couple of quotes from your evidence from that case to you, and I have them here on a sheet of paper which I would like to put on the ELMO. And I would ask you to comment on the quotes, and these are quotes either from your reports that you had written at the time or from your testimony in the Naletilic/Martinovic case. The quotes are both in English and in B/C/S. There's five of them, and you can either read them from the paper or -- but they will also appear on the screen. Let me just read out the first quote which people can also follow from the screen: "Therefore the views on a war are in many respects similar, which does not mean they are accurate. For Serbs, it was a preventive war with the purpose to prevent their own experience of 1941, and a war with an objective - an attempt to create an integral Serbian state. For Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was a war for emancipation, with a wish to integrate with the parent country." Sir, do you recall this particular paragraph which was in your final consideration of your expert's report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I don't remember, but it is quite possible that I did write that. Do you have my report, itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was prepared in 2001, and in those days, in preparing that report, I stand by it 90 percent and more. But since then things have changed, and especially new documents were found, and I was able to look at the archives, the archives of President Tudjman. I had occasion to read many transcripts. So if a conclusion -- this conclusion was something I actually said at the time, today I don't think it is in accord with what I found out later. After having seen 200 and more transcripts and comparing that with what happened on the ground, I think that the basic aim of the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina was an entity of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: One moment, please, Mr. Bos. Your Honour, this question, of course, in my respectful submission, was outside the examination-in-chief. I don't object on that basis. I think, of course, Mr. Bos can proceed, as far as we're concerned, and test the credibility of this witness. However, it is somewhat difficult to recall an expert report written seven years previously. The witness has intimated on one reading that he wishes to have sight of the report, and if my friend wishes to pursue this, I think it's only fair that the actual report of this witness be put to him and the context of whatever is put can be properly understood. I think that's the fair way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no problems for this witness to actually have this report shown to him as well. It's in our bundle under Exhibit 3D 00715. I'm afraid there's only an English version. The report was only submitted in English in the Naletilic/Martinovic case, and that's why I took out a couple of quotes which were then also translated into Bosnian -- B/C/S. And I think, in fact, that the Stojic Defence counsel included this report also in their bundle of exhibits, if I understood --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Bos doesn't object, my learned friend, Ms. Nozica, has passed to me the same report, but in a language that the witness understands. Perhaps he could be shown that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, you will get the report in your own language, so you can -- you don't need the binder. So, Mr. Marijan, from what I understood from your answer, it seems that your position has changed since you gave testimony in Tuta Stela, so let me read out the quotes that are related to this point and ask you, on all these quotes, whether you still agree with your position or not. This is the second quote, and I'll read that out as well. It says -- this is actually from your -- no, this is again from your expert report, and it reads as follows: "The politics of the Republic of Croatia," and at trial you corrected that to read "the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina," so: "The politics of Bosnia-Herzegovina towards Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, in which one of the constitutional nations are also the Croats, obviously had a desire for unification into an integral Croatian state. That is indisputable. The only disputable thing is the interpretation of the manner in which it was sought to be achieved." So here you say it was obviously there was a desire for unification and that it was indisputable. Are you now saying that seven years later, your view has completely changed on this point?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my personal opinion, when I was writing this, I didn't refer to any documents, so this was my own personal conclusion. I always had the impression, and even now I think that the average Croat in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially the area in which I live, that Croatia for them had priority over Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is due to various circumstances, especially their status in the last 40 years, and this is understandable to me, up to a point. As for this particular point, I have written seven or eight books. My eighth book is about to be published, and more than 30 papers. I was never satisfied with them. I would always revise them and change them. So this was my viewpoint at that point in time, and at the time I didn't have access to many things, and some things appeared to me to be simpler at the time, and probably also under the influence of a massive campaign that is still being waged in Croatia today, and probably this led me to reach that conclusion. And as I said in my previous answer, having seen a large quantity of documents since then, have led me to correct my views, and this is something that will happen constantly. And history never ends, it's a process, and this is my view of that history.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's see how -- on your next quote you talk about, you know, the basis for making -- making these conclusions, and this is actually what you said in your testimony: "This opinion of mine," and referring to the paragraph above, "is based on my personal contacts. I did not meet more than two Croats from Bosnia who were not geared towards Zagreb, who did not turn their eyes towards Zagreb." Do you recall this evidence, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would object. Now we're talking about Croats, the individuals there. I mean, I don't think you could go to Greece and find a single Greek that doesn't look to Constantinople and think that it doesn't belong to Greece. It doesn't means that Greeks are going to be attacking Turkey to try to take over Asia Minor. I mean, what the Greeks think about Constantinople is no different than what the Croats might think about in -- from Bosnia and Herzegovina, but certain areas, that has nothing to do with policy or politics. It has to do with individual wishes and aspirations and their understanding of history, so I would object to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This is evidence that from -- from Mr. Marijan, himself, from his testimony. I'm just asking him to clarify what he meant by saying this, and I don't see why he couldn't answer on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's irrelevant, it's irrelevant, Your Honour. He says he's talking about -- he didn't meet two Croats --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Two Croats from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From Bosnia, they're individuals, and they're entitled to have their aspirations and their entitled to have their understanding of the history. That has nothing to do with policies and politics. That's my point of view, and that's why I mention Greeks looking at Const antinople.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've just heard what Mr. Karnavas has said, you've heard Mr. Bos' question. In your report, from which I have before me, and what you said in the Naletilic case, you spoke about the Croats. Now, was that a general feeling or, as was said by Mr. Karnavas, were there individuals having that point of view without that being a general for that matter? You are the one who said and testified in that case and wrote that report. What kind of additional information can you provide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't recall this, but I probably did say this. Maybe the words are not all there, but the -- I don't think the gist of it has changed. This is my personal feeling. It's difficult to say now, during the collapse of Yugoslavia from 1990 until 2001, when this was prepared, it is difficult to say how many Croats I met. Anyway, the majority of Croats I was in touch with, there may have been 100.000 [as interpreted] or 2.000, certainly not more than 5.000, but less, so this is a question taking us back to the past, why the average Croat did not see Bosnia-Herzegovina as their homeland. I think it would take a lot of time for me to explain this. I can give you my example. I'm from Livno. It takes about an hour and a half to two hours to reach Sarajevo by car. To reach Zagreb, it takes three to four hours. Why did my father build a house close to Zagreb and not close to Sarajevo? This was in the 1970s already. So this question touches upon mentality, and Livno has a majority of Croats, and it was a personnel issue that the president of the municipality had to be a Croat. All the other positions were held by other ethnicities. So the environment within which I moved had a strong feeling of inequality, and this went on until 1990, 1991, and this, in my view, explains why I said this and why the majority of Croats, I don't think they have changed their opinion. There are very few Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina that I met who are not turned towards Zagreb. Madam Nozica is one of them. I am saying that the majority sees it this way. I don't see what the problem is. It's a problem that goes back to the past, a problem of enormous injustice, and this cannot be remedied overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... say the counsel, but as there are several, I don't know who you refer to. I think you referred to Ms. Nozica, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yeah, you got it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. In the transcript, it does say "Ms. Nozica." My colleague has a question to put. Mr. Bos, the Registrar has told me that you've used up your 15 minutes, so you'll have to put the last question, I think. But first of all, my colleague would like to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, my question is a more theoretical nature. Mr. Karnavas has not without some reason, of course, said that what you refer to here are opinions of individuals, and that, says Mr. Karnavas, is not relevant, and in fact what we are dealing with, what is important, is what the authorities, the official Herceg-Bosna, was aiming at. Now, I would like you to explain whether, and how, if so, the opinion of individuals is relevant in order to assess the aim of the political entity, and even whether, in fact, you are saying that it is an acceptable method of historical research to rely or at least to take into account what the majority in a certain territory wants? I hope the question is not too complicated. It's not too simple, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is a logical fact, in my opinion, that a political leadership, any political leadership - we're not discussing whether that will be Bosnian Croats political leadership or any political leadership - in a certain way such leadership must keep their ear to the ground and take into account the feelings of an electorate, so to speak, but let me go back to the time when I was preparing this first report. I completely ignored the existence of the Republic of Croatia or the Republic of Serbian Krajina in the Republic of Croatia which determined certain political aims, and political aims are, in a certain way, public. They are made public, being uttered at public meetings or closed meetings of higher political echelons. To me, as a historian, and I did say this because it was my opinion, solely my opinion, and it should be taken as such, there is a possibility to find a Croat who will have a different opinion, because it was formed by different people. I participated at the HVO three times in three different time intervals. Not once as a soldier have I or my contacts or the environment of the unit where I was clearly told what were the political aims of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna, whether those aims were clearly stated, put on paper in a form of a proclamation, enumerated, and that is an answer of sorts, in my opinion, about those matters. So as a soldier who was expected to fight, I was not told what I was fighting about, except, and this is not to be sneezed at, defending my own municipality. And the next-door community from the front-line was my home village, so you do not need any epistles stating high moral reasons to defend that turf. Your Honour, your question was a complicated one, so I'm not sure if my answer suffices. If necessary, I can elaborate upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, we could go on at length, and I don't think that's the purpose, to hold a historical methodological seminar here. Just if I look at the transcript, on page 14, line 13 and 14, the English reads: "Not once as a soldier have I or my contacts or the environmental of the unit where I was clearly -- where I was clearly told what were the political aims." I wonder whether you said that or whether you meant to say, "We were never told what the political aims of the war were." Could you make that clear, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see the transcript, but it certainly has not been put on record clearly. As I said, me and my unit were never given black-on-white or uttered from somebody coming from higher echelons stating what the aims -- the goals of that were, and this is a matter of strategy which I don't believe Herceg-Bosna had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I believe that what you've said is important. You were one of the few soldiers who has been here to testify. We know that General Praljak will be testifying; Petkovic as well. You are an expert and also a soldier, so your previous answer that you gave to my colleague's question prompts me to add a clarification. You were saying that you were a soldier in the Livno region and that you did not leave it. I would like to know the brigade commander, the deputies, in fact the entire military environment, when they brought you together for a briefing, before you went into combat, or when you had meetings, when there were communications between them and you, did they say, "We are facing an attack, in which case we have to defend ourselves," or did they say things along the lines of, "We want our independence, we must recognise Herceg-Bosna," or did they say, "The Republic is in jeopardy because there's a siege in Sarajevo, there are the Serbs," and so on and so forth? In other words, did your superiors -- did the commanders have a political discourse where they explained to the soldiers what they were doing or did they tell you nothing? Did they just say, "There is an enemy and we have to defend or attack"? According to your recollection, what was the message you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the first two campaigns of the HVO concerned Livno, the first two. The third one, I was a professional soldier and falls outside this purview, which was in 1994-1995, outside the area of Livno. Two or three times, I was in the area of Gornji Vakuf. But as far as your question is concerned, I have a good memory, but I cannot really recall anybody giving us a speech on these matters. That is the problem. Starting with the battalion commander and the brigade commander, I knew the brigade commander from before the war, he was in the Territorial Defence, but I can't recall ever seeing him during wartime, which speaks volumes about the situation. We never received any political message. Your question was specific as to my case. Maybe somebody else appearing as a witness may tell you a different story, but my story is as I've relayed it to you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, as you tell us that you have not been briefed by the superiors on the aims, I imagine -- I have difficulties in imagining that it would have been otherwise, that you wanted -- you made your own assessment of the situation and you had a feeling what you were fighting for, and I suppose - I don't think this is far-fetched - that you talked with others in your environment, your social environment, military environment, about what you all were fighting for, what your aims were. Could you tell us something about this? Have you got a recollection as to whether there was a goal that was predominant in your minds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not easy to go back in one's mind 17 or 18 years. I came to the HVO on the day when the conflict in Kupres started, the 3rd of April. I used a regular bus line from Zagreb to Livno. There were four or five passengers in all. I went there because my family -- because of my father and mother, and I believe I mentioned it on the first day of my testimony. That was my motive. What was important for me then was to keep my -- intact that part of me which was connected to that place, part of my history, and this was my motive then. I -- there was no need for anybody to tell me or to boost my morale about that. I believe that I had high morale. At the time, I was a student. We were a student unit, and we were specific in terms of our thinking. We know that current affairs or current politicking was not our focus. Judge Antonetti asked me about that, and I don't believe that we even reacted to the proclamation of Herceg-Bosna in August of 1993. It would have stuck in my memory had we had a particular reaction to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Your answer, Mr. Marijan, seems to cover the beginning of your activity as a soldier. Then, after a certain time, the Serb attack was stopped and the danger from the Serbs moved into the background, and that the main opponent were the Muslims. At that time, did you still feel that you had to defend your family in Livno against the Muslims, even when you were sent to for Gornji Vakuf, or did you -- did you develop your ideas about what the war was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in Livno we were not threatened by Muslims because of the conflagration, lay of the terrain, compared to those at other places. What I remembered about the conflict was that we were unclear as to the purpose of that conflict, of that war. With regard to Gornji Vakuf, we held our lines in Croatian-populated villages, and the predominant way of thinking was that we were a bit upset because there were no locals of those villages there at the time. I recall that we did not like it. We felt that we were doing a job that we thought the local people should be doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, I told you that you have used up your time. If you have one last question, please put it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I can then conclude with the last quote that I have on that page, which follows from that other quote, and it sort of relates to what you just said, that there were no higher echelons stating the political aims. Sir, if I can put that last quote to you as my last question, this is what you stated in your expert report: "Croatian politics towards Bosnia-Herzegovina obviously had a starting point in the assumption that Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot survive. One can agree with that or not agree. The views of Franjo Tudjman on Bosnia and Herzegovina were not a secret. He did not believe in its viability, which can be documented by his statements and, less reliably, by the claims of various witnesses of the history."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall this evidence? And let me ask you a concrete question: What are the statements that you are referring to made by Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was uttered in 2001. At that time, in Croatia certain transcripts started to emerge for current political purposes. The first was the 27th of December, 2001, and then I believe that this is public knowledge, and a series of transcripts were unearthed, and Tudjman himself issued a number of statements. He was a person who spoke before thinking, in political terms, if it could be put that way. I thought that he was transgressing at the boundaries of politics and was talking too much, but in none of the transcripts did it emerge that he had made an agreement with Slobodan Milosevic on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Fifteen years have passed since the Dayton Accords, and of all my statements that I had issued then, this is the one that I would stick by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I see you're standing. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to know when the witness states a series of statements by President Tudjman, at least those should be -- should be said when and where those statements were issued, so that we can refer back to them down the road. I'm going to provide testimony, so I will need to know when a president of the state issued a statement, where they were recorded, and where we can find them. Otherwise, we are just a discussion club.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that President Tudjman made a number of statements, but you didn't give us the dates of those statements, so we don't know precisely what you're referring to. I presume that you have taken a look at the presidential transcripts. I don't know whether you can give us a precise date. Can you, can you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe I was prompted by poor interpretation. I said it could be corroborated by his statements, I mean, President Tudjman's. There were a number of his statements published in daily newspapers. I cannot recall specific dates. I know that some of the them have been published in a publication, a book, Croatian words to -- the external words. Some were uttered at SFRY Presidency meetings, sessions, but I can't really specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But you've been talking about this statement, but you haven't said one thing about the content of the statement. What did Mr. Tudjman actually say in these statements? I haven't heard anything about that.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, first, Tudjman's politics should be researched and studied in detail. Otherwise, one could draw conclusions misguided on the basis of a number of his statements. My opinion is that Tudjman's policy was geared towards the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina being given an entity. I believe that he discussed this with Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Milosevic. In my opinion, such matters were not unknown, and the International Community shared this opinion. It constantly divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into three entities, and this influence on President Tudjman should not be ignored and should be further researched, because there is a fourth dimension to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will leave it at this, and thank you for your answers, Mr. Marijan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to point out that on page 19, I believe it was line 13, there was a reference to a presidential transcript, and the gentleman indicated it was 2001. It was the 17 December, and we have here "2001." Perhaps he could give us the correct date. I know the date of that particular transcript, but perhaps the witness could tell us which one he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, most probably I did not state -- state it. This was 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have just one more administrative matter. The two pages of the quotes, if I could get an IC number for this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document shall be given Exhibit IC 00905. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, are we introducing the entire pages or just the quotes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because the quotes are in the transcript already. I haven't -- I mean, I know that -- I haven't looked at the transcript, and if I wanted to pull a fast one - I'm not suggesting that one is being pulled on us - but if there's anything else in those pages that haven't been put to the witness, then obviously they shouldn't come in. The quotes are in the record. The record speaks for itself, and I see no reason why we need those -- an IC number for those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's correct that I read them out, so I'm happy to leave it with the records and no IC number. It's not necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, so it's not necessary. Registrar, we will not give it a number, particularly as the number did not come up on the screen. So, Registrar, there is to be no number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The number -- Exhibit IC 00905 [Realtime transcript read in error "975"] is withdrawn from the record. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have one last question that I'd like to put to you, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction to the transcript. 905 and not "975."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, the IC number is 905 and not 975. That is the number to be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have one last question to you, which concerns the conclusion of paragraph 126. I presume that for you, it was important to read this in paragraph 126, where you say that the Croat Community or the Herceg-Bosna Republic came from the dismantling of former Yugoslavia, and there was a crisis and so on. And you conclude by saying: "... because it was impossible to find an agreement with the other peoples," the three; in other words, Serbs, Croats and Muslims. And in reading that conclusion, and bearing in mind what you said earlier on, concerning the Serb Republic of the Krajina, I would like to put the following question to you: On the basis of all of the documents you have seen, all of the works that you have written, the testimony in the Naletilic case, I'd like to know whether what happened in Herceg-Bosna, Herzegovina particularly, is it the same type of event as those that occurred in Krajina, in the Serb Krajina of Croatia, or in Republika Srpska? In ex-Yugoslavia, was there not identical behaviour in regions -- in zones that had a dominant ethnic group where a mode of behaviour was followed which led to this type of entity? Is this a matter that has been the subject of study, of reflection, and what is your personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was an attempt, particularly in daily newspapers, to draw a sign of equality between the Republic of Srpska Krajina in Croatia and Herceg-Bosna in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The problem there is I don't believe that this comparison is tenable. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croats were a constituent people. In the Republic of Croatia, the Serbs became an ethnic minority. I don't know whether you know the background of these events, the whole story in the context of the disintegration of ex-Yugoslavia, and its fulcrum in the issue, when Serbia started denying an ethnic minority their constitutional rights in Kosovo, and this of course influenced other groups and resulted in a fear infiltrating the relationship between a minority and a majority in a certain area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer. Ms. Nozica, the Court has granted you one hour, but we would like to remind you that in the questions you will be putting as part of your redirect, these questions must be related to the questions put by the Prosecutor. So for us to know precisely where we're going, it would be much better if you were to say, for instance, "On page X, line Y, the Prosecutor put such and such a question. Witness, you gave this answer, and now I would like to put the following question to you," so that we can establish a clear link between the cross-examination and your redirect.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. I just wish to point out that my cross-examination will not relate exclusively to the cross-examination of the Prosecutor, but that it will partly relate to the cross-examinations of other Defence counsels, and I would appeal to the Trial Chamber to allow me, in this first part, my questions be directed to the questions put by the Prosecutor to the witness today. For this, I don't need any documents. And then, if possible, I would ask for us to have a break, once I complete the first part of my questions, so that we might distribute my documents, so as to make the best of the time available, because I will certainly be using my time and using it up after the break. I would like to ask Your Honours whether you agree with this methodology. If not, give me a minute to distribute the documents straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed as you suggested. Put your questions on the basis of the Prosecutor's questions, then we'll have a break and you will distribute some documents, and you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, in the report that you filed in the Naletilic case, did you delve into the question of aid to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in arming, training, and other facilities to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1991 onwards?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I did. I may have just mentioned it without going into any detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, I'm afraid that I may be more familiar with your report than you are, so I would like you to look into that report during the break. Yes, you did study those issues, and they have been elaborated in your report. There's an intervention on page 22 -- no, I'm sorry, page 25, line 22, whether you delved into the question of aid of the Croatian Community to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Marijan, you said today, and this follows from the quote from your report, when you spoke about the position of Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is recorded in line 10 -- or, rather, page 10, line 20, the Prosecutor quoted from that report and you said that you were voicing your own opinion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You then also said that after providing that report, you gained possession of other presidential transcripts and other documents, due to which you changed your view as expressed during the trial of the Naletilic/Martinovic case; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to correct it. I didn't gain possession; I just had occasion to read transcripts. It is only the Prosecution that can gain possession of the documents, but I did have occasion to read them, due to circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me now turn back to the questions addressed in this report, the documents and transcripts, and everything else that you had at your disposal at the present time, because I acknowledge what you say, that as an historian -- a historian, giving assessments of past events is a process, and that it cannot be established with reliability at any particular point in time. So I'm asking you, at this point in time, on the basis of all the evidence that you have reviewed in this case, is your opinion the same as you presented it today, and that is that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not have, as its aim, the secession of parts of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I expressed that opinion quite clearly earlier on, on the basis of all the documents I've seen up to the present, that the aim of the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a constituent unit within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me now go a little forward. In the course of 1992 and 1993, did you have occasion to come across memorandums of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and whether it was quite clear in those documents where the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna belongs?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw, I don't remember a memorandum that was printed and used. I think it was customary, in my brigade in 1993 and 1994, the heading always started with: "Bosnia and Herzegovina," and then: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: For the benefit of the transcript, could you be more precise in your answer? Did you see a single printed memorandum without "Bosnia-Herzegovina" heading it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the memorandums I saw, and I saw many, always started with "The Republic of Herceg-Bosna" at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A quick follow-up question, Witness. We heard a witness before who was a soldier, like you, and he explained that in his unit, he had insignias on his uniform. On the one hand, he had the sign of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; on the other, the sign of the HVO. With regard to your own uniforms, could you tell us what kind of insignias you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my wartime uniform in 1992 and 1993 is at home. I keep it as memorabilia, and I don't think there are any insignia on it. I didn't like to put insignia of the brigade or anything else. I simply didn't feel like it. I didn't want to attach insignia. I collect these things, and I did see many insignia. I collect them. And I think I said on the first day that at least in 1992, in Livno, the battalion received orders to remove all insignia which were contrary to the HVO. And if I delve into the issue more deeply, I think it was mainly directed against the HOS and not against the BH Army, because the HOS, in the territory where I was, was considered a greater problem. So in 1992, the Muslims in Livno - maybe not all of them, but most of them - did wear both insignia. Sometimes there was the TO insignia rather than the BH Army insignia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Ms. Nozica continues, I just want to make an objection to the last question that was put by Ms. Nozica, which was an extremely leading question, and I -- in redirect I think she should be not asking leading questions, but open-ended questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nozica, do avoid putting leading questions. You're a great professional. You must be able to achieve the same result with open questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. Judge Trechsel wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Marijan, you have said that you have never seen a document without -- an official document of Herceg-Bosna which did not have "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" on it. I suppose you have seen all the documents that figure in your footnotes, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, Your Honour. My question was quite different and very precise. I asked about memorandums, if a document had a memorandum. I didn't ask about documents that did not have a memorandum, so I think that is why the witness said what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, I didn't use that, but you are aware, Witness, that there are letterheads printed formal which said "Hrvatska Sjednica Herceg-Bosna" [phoen] and "Hrvatsko Vijece Obranje," [phoen] but no reference to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that was very rare. I think the vast majority had the words "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." They were printed. And this is a question of archives or the general affairs of a unit. A large number of documents were written on an ordinary typewriter. In that case, the copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just for the record, I'm referring to document 2D 01356. That was the example that I found now, after looking for it for two or three minutes in a binder I picked at random. Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in continuation of my re-examination, the witness will be shown several documents, and we will see documents without this heading. Let me proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, in answer to a question by His Honour Judge Antonetti, you said, and that is how Their Honours understood you to say, that in 1992, you came to your home in Livno to defend your own town and your parents. I think that is what you actually said. And you said that this was an attack by the Serbian army. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was an attack by the Serbian army. If something is not clear, I can say that the area where we were, the neighbouring municipalities, Glamoc, with a majority Serb population, our trenches and defence lines were about 150 metres within our municipal boundaries, so those lines were along the cadaster boundaries of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, when we're talking about 1993, your second tour of duty, when Judge Trechsel asked you about this, did you go to Gornji Vakuf to carry out an attack against the Muslims or for some other reason? I do not wish to put a leading question and thus bring you back to what you said on the first day of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in Gornji Vakuf, we -- our positions were always in a village that had a majority Croat population, which means defence. In those days, the BH Army was exerting strong pressure on Gornji Vakuf, and the front-line was very strange, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And my final question --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think in this case it would be helpful if we got the exact month in 1993 that Mr. Marijan was in Gornji Vakuf in order to confuse -- not to get confused. At the moment, it only says "1993."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Marijan has indicated the time with precision, but I don't mind if he answer it again, and let it be in the time of my dear colleague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't remember the exact date, but it was in the late autumn. I think it was late autumn and there was snowfall. And then the second area, I was at home for Christmas, and the third was just before the Washington Agreement, if my memory's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, earlier on -- before Ms. Nozica asked you the question, I wanted to ask it myself and now I do have to ask it. Earlier on, in order to explain why you went to Gornji Vakuf, you said that you went there to guard villages, and you said "because the inhabitants were no longer there," that's what I understood, and you were frustrated to see that they were gone. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this was during the evidence presented by the Prosecutor, and we were unhappy that in a fit of panic, able-bodied people had fled, and there was the question as to why we are going there when the local inhabitants are not ready to defend themselves. That was our view at the time, but now, to be a soldier in Gornji Vakuf was far more difficult a task than to be a soldier in Livno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good, but this, your answer, prompts me to think of something I hadn't thought of before. In the concept of defence in Bosnia and Herzegovina, be it in Livno or Gornji Vakuf, in terms of defence, is it first the inhabitants that must defend the area; is that a general principle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for a long time, maybe up to the summer or the late -- late summer of 1993, that is how the HVO functioned. Each unit, even though they were called brigades, according to military rules, it is a unit that is not linked to a particular territory but can go further afield. But most municipalities, virtually all of them in Herzegovina and this part of Bosnia where I come from, the defences were mostly a local affair. In Gornji Vakuf, because of difficulties and problems, the brigade lost some effectives, and I don't know whether it even had two companies. What its real ability was could be seen in 1994. After the war against the Muslims, it was reduced to a battalion. So that was what it should have been, regardless of the name that it had as a brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if defence was a local affair, which is what you said; in Capljina it should be defended by locals, in Prozor it should be locals, the same for Mostar, Livno, Gornji Vakuf, always locals. Now, to put all this together, to organise defence as was conceived by the Croats in Herzegovina, was that basically a locally-based, municipality-based defence, and in this context the military component of the HVO, with the head of staff, et cetera, what did they do as part of this general principle or in relation to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The role of higher levels of command in the operation zone and the Main Staff of Herceg-Bosna at the time was to strengthen defence lines where they were threatened. If somebody attacks you, they first assess your weak spots and then they concentrate their forces there. Practically, one takes a look at Main Staff documents in the latter part of 1993, one gains an impression of a fire-fighter skipping with a bucket of water here and there, trying to put out fires all over the place. Very small forces would be brought to a place, manoeuvres with one or two artillery pieces, be it cannon or mortars. It was very difficult to withdraw a brigade-size unit from one place to shore up the defence of another place, and this is the gist of what I was saying about the local type of defence in Herceg-Bosna. But this was not particularly just to Herceg-Bosna. I perceived the same thing in other armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, if the soldiers in Prozor had been told, "You have to go to Livno or Mostar," would they have been reluctant to do so? Would they have said, well, it was not their problem, that their only goal was to defend Prozor and not to go anywhere else? Was that the general state of mind of all soldiers, such as you, who were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as per decree, each soldier of the armed forces of the HZ-HB had the duty to serve at any territory, but very often we had refusals by a whole unit to go somewhere. So there was -- there were efforts to convince them higher levels of command had to be involved, and very often the whole thing was more for resembling begging than to go somewhere, rather than convincing them that they should do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, we have five minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Only two more questions concerning this topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, please, I've just taken a look at your report. That's 3D 715. I'm not going to recall it, but I'd like to refresh your memory. You said, in your report, that the Croatian state sent armaments to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina through the HVO, and as per your then research, this continued until mid-March of 1993. Do you recall discussing this? If so, say it; if not, I will go to another topic.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after this text, I prepared an addendum to this report, and I never meant to go back to it, to revisit it. I found some documents that corrected my opinion, and that was published in Mostar at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And the final question about this: You discussed the structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You spoke about today's circumstances, and you spoke about the fourth conflict, and this is why my question is going to be very specific. Did all Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina have a single opinion as to the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or whether there was among Muslims or Bosniaks there were inter-Bosniak conflicts arising from differing opinions about the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a specific quality of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. I have difficulties linking this question either to the report or to the cross-examination by the Prosecutor. I think it's outside the scope of your redirect.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I beg to differ. I think this is what the witness was discussing when he said, asked by His Honour Antonetti, as far as I can remember, when he was asked about his conclusion in his report about the peoples in Yugoslavia could not reach an agreement, the witness discussed Bosnia-Herzegovina, different views held by Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, and he mentioned the fourth conflict or the fourth side. I do believe that this is what the witness meant. And since, in his report, the witness stated that no agreement could be reached on the structure of Yugoslavia, asked about that by the Prosecutor on how the Croats saw the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now I, following from that, asked the witness whether all the Muslims or Bosniaks had a single view of the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina or whether, during that conflict or war, there was a fourth conflict which stemmed from such differing views, and which he, himself, mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we should ask the witness. Did you also study the opinion of the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not deal with Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina in detail, but each document I had possession of, I read. There's no doubt about that, and I mentioned that in my previous report. The Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina were specific in that there was an internal conflict among their ranks, unsurpassed by a difference of opinion in any other side. I'm not sure whether I said a fourth conflict. I mentioned that the International Community drew lines on the map as well, and they cannot benefit from an amnesty of what they were doing in the overall scheme of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you say -- what I'm specifically interested in, in the inter-Bosniak conflict, what was the reason for it? I don't want to give a leading question?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find enough documents. What is the matter here is that Cazin Krajina and Fikret Abdic, and the fact that that conflict did erupt, means that Mr. Abdic's opinion differed from that of the -- that held by Alija Izetbegovic, which was a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Abdic favoured a view of greater autonomy, and this entered the title of that entity around Bihac and Cazin.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you share with us the title or the name of that territory controlled by Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Thank you, Your Honours. I will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The session resumes. I believe, Ms. Alaburic, you wish to put a question; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I did not want to ask any questions. And, procedurally, I'm in no position to ask questions. I just wish to say that at the end of today's session, I will have an oral submission to make, if there will be sufficient time for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you. So that was for the oral motion, the oral submission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Following your instructions, I will make a reference, before each group of questions, to what I'm anchoring my questions on from the cross-examination. The first question I'm going to ask of Mr. Marijan refers to his answer recorded on page 35720, line 13 to 25. I would just like to note, since Mr. Marijan does not have that part of the transcript, that it refers to his explanation about the authorities of the HVO of the HZ-HB; more precisely, his explanation about the difference between the position of the president of the HVO HZ-HB and the Presidency of the then-state, as he put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, in your answers you made reference to a statutory decision. I would like to ask you to take a look at the first document in the binder, and that is P 00303, and I would like to ask you to continue your answer in this vein, if you wish so, about the authorities or competences within the HVO of HZ-HB. Mr. Marijan, asked about my learned colleague Karnavas's, you reconfirmed what you said on several occasions, that you were not a lawyer, and for that reason I would like you to take a look at this decision and to refer to the sections or articles that you thought governed the issue of competencies and not to comment on it in any way. Please take a look and read through the section or article that you thought governed authorities or competencies.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I referred to Articles 14 and Article 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you like to read those articles, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 14: "Croatian Defence Council performs the supervision of its own work and municipal HVO. HVO may rescind the acts of the bodies from the previous article." And Article 9: "The presidents of the HVO manages the work of the HVO and is responsible for its work. It secures a unity of political and security of work of HVO, effects cooperation with other bodies of the HZ-HB, and directs the work of HVO as a whole and its constituent parts. The president of the HVO signs the documents of the HVO. The Presidency of the HVO, in the case of absence or circumstances of them not being able to, is replaced by a deputy."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, this -- is this everything you wanted to say during cross-examination as to the competencies of the president of the HVO and the head of the department, because this was the gist of the question, and the question was about the selection, election, appointment, and authority to sign? Do you wish to add anything? I have many questions to ask you and very limited time, so please make your answers very short.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall everything I said, but when I referred to the statutory decision, these are the articles that I meant, and this is all I have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to inform Their Honours that in the following group of questions, and I will make it clear when this is going to finish, I will refer to my learned colleague Alaburic's questions during her cross-examination, which were followed upon by the Prosecutor, and these refer to the relationship between the head of the department -- head of Defence Department, in terms of the basis for the structure of the Defence Department, and in this connection please take a look at the following document, P 00806, and that refers also to the item 9 that you were asked about. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My learned colleague Alaburic asked you about the penultimate paragraph. I would start with the penultimate paragraph, in terms of principled and concrete competencies. I -- we have a different -- we have a different document retrieved. I wanted to retrieve P 00586, and I see the same mistake in the transcript. So it's P 00586. So my colleague Alaburic asked you about the penultimate paragraph of Article 9, which reads: "Within the remit of principled and specific competencies from the president of the HVO of Herceg-Bosna, the chief of General Staff is superior to the Croatian Armed Forces Defence Council." Would you please explain about those competencies and this superior position? What did you mean by "command of the Croatian Defence Council"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this I meant only the municipal staffs. Nothing else comes to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Since my colleague continued asking you questions about the last paragraph of this article, which discusses which tasks brigade commanders, whether they would be subordinated or responsible to the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces, and in which aspects they were subordinated to the head of the Defence Department and chief of the Main Staff, and in -- and I quote: "In accordance with the powers described above --" Thank you, Your Honour. So please read paragraph 3 of this article, in terms of those competencies which elaborates upon them.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These -- well, it would be best for me to read it out: "The chief of the Main Staff will be responsible to the head of the department, proposing and implement measures for all administrative tasks and issues relating to the budget and material supplies and consumption and general organisation of civilian life as well as organisation of the armed forces." This is the remit of the head of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In which tasks commander -- chief of the General Staff is responsible to the president of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, because this question misinterprets paragraph 9. Those words refer to the responsibilities of the chief of the Main Staff and not to the remit of the head of the Defence Department. The remit of the head of the Defence Department is governed by all the other paragraphs up until paragraph 9, so what the witness is reading out concerns the responsibilities of the chief of the Main Staff. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I maintain my position, that interpretation of regulations, irrespective of how we, she, or the witness may interpret them, will be subject to the assessment of the Bench on what the regulations what and what actions they engendered. I would like to continue. I'm reading out what is written. I would like to ask the witness to continue reading why chief of the Main Staff is directly responsible and accountable to the president of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The chief of the Main Staff is responsible directly to the president of the HVO, of the HZ-HB, in all issues relating to supreme command, unit organisation, strategic and operative plans, and the use of the armed forces in time of war or peace."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, on several occasions during your chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: For the third time in transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the defendant. Microphone for the accused, please. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: It is for the third time in the same page, when counsel said very clearly "president of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," in transcript we have wording "President of HVO." This is the third time on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is a big distinction, this is a very big distinction, and I'm shocked that it is being allowed to be -- you know, either counsel is not picking it up or the gentleman is doing it on purpose, and I would ask that they slow down so the interpreters can get it right. But there is a vast difference between president of the HVO HZ-HB and the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, vast difference. And it's not a surprise -- it is not a surprise that Mr. Stojic is trying to blame -- trying to blame Jadranko Prlic, and trying to put him -- put Jadranko Prlic on top of him. And so I would appreciate that if we slow down and be precise, and if there is a problem, to correct it. Counsel has an obligation to correct the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It might perhaps not be entirely politically correct, but it would make things easier if we said "Boban" and "Prlic" instead of titles that bear some similarity and therefore are prone to be mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Prlic, as he understands both languages, he correctly conveyed what Defence counsel said and what the witness said. I did not use the term "HVO" once, but "the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." So if my learned friend sees a mistake in the transcript, not to blame me, and especially not Mr. Stojic, that we are imputing anything to his client. I said clearly, and this was confirmed by Mr. Prlic, I said "the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." There's no need to increase the tension, because we will not achieve anything. Anyone who notices a mistake in the transcript should react immediately. I have no problem in apologising if the mistake is mine. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just wanted to intervene in support of what Mr. Karnavas was saying. We should not mix up the president of the HVO and the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. At the same time, I should also like to support Ms. Nozica. In other words, there's no need to add to the tension. Mr. Karnavas has said that Mr. Stojic was placing Mr. Prlic above him, and that is a sort of interpretation I think we should avoid at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There was just an error in the translation. It has been corrected, and we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, my learned friend Alaburic showed you some documents, and some were shown by my learned friend the Prosecutor. I will cover some documents now that you didn't have time to comment on. So let us comment on them very briefly, and will you briefly answer my question: Do they belong to the responsibilities of the head of the Defence Department that we have read on the internal structure? And this relates to communications with the brigades and other units of the HVO. Let us first look at document P 00600. It is the next one on the list, and will you, please, when you find it, tell us whether this document in any way implies that Mr. Stojic did not act in any sense contrary to his authority? This document doesn't have a memorandum, but still we have typewritten the words "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." I have looked through all the documents in the binder, those with the letterhead have these words, and even this one, which has been typed, has these same words. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I recognise this, so it will not be necessary to repeat it. I must have fallen on an exception. I give you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and the exception confirms the rule; isn't it so? That's what we say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, from these two sentences, it is difficult to say what was the purpose of the meeting. We have listed previously the competencies of Mr. Stojic, so he is entitled to communicate, and to be able to provide a clear, unequivocal answer we would need to have the result of this meeting. One could always ask ourselves whether the meeting took place at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Will you please look at the next document, please. If you wish to give the same answer as for the previous one, say so. The document is P 00799.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please look at the next document, P 00804. This is a transfer, Bruno Busic is going from Posuski, and tell me, there's a date, and tell me whether the communication is contrary to the competencies of communication between Mr. Stojic and this person.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an order regulating the deployment of the regiment or its accommodation and movement from Posuski Gradac, from the school, to the Heliodrom barracks, which is within the terms of reference of Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you now look at the document shown to you by Ms. Alaburic and the Prosecutor, P 01098. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said you would have liked to see documents to show which were the authority over the civilian police. We have discussed this at some length. No, I'm sorry, I'm sorry, my mistake. I went too fast. We are talking here about an order about all settlements, and movement of persons in uniform bearing weapons are being prohibited. Only official persons may bear weapons outside of the front-lines. Tell me, does this order in any way go beyond the frameworks of Mr. Bruno Stojic's competencies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is Mr. Bruno Stojic is authorised to issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document, P 03146. It's a document dated the 3rd of July, 1993. It relates to the Kresimir Brigade from Livno, and a military police unit is centred to be relocated to Mostar. Would you say that in any way this letter -- yes, it is an order. Does it go beyond the scope of the authority of Mr. Stojic in the way you have described them in your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just add this is the Petar Kresimir Brigade, which is just a transmission. This relates to the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police. Mr. Andabak was the commander of that battalion, so Mr. Stojic is addressing directly the Military Police Battalion, which is not, by formation, part of this brigade, and I think it is within his competencies. So we now come to the next document, P 05232.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic, if I look at the transcript, it is you who give the answer, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is both my mistake and your mistake. I'm not Ms. Alaburic, I'm Ms. Nozica, and indeed the witness's answer has not appeared on the transcript. Shall we ask him to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this order, 503146, that this order is in line with the authority of Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you shed some light on this? You have just said that the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police did not belong to the Kresimir Brigade, your brigade. I'm trying to understand here. I believe that in a military organisation, any brigade has attached to it a unit of military police, so how is it that the 2nd Battalion is not part of the brigade? Did it come from Mostar just temporarily? Was it resubordinated to the brigade, and then was it decided to send it back to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Petar Kresimir Brigade had a platoon of military police. Here, in brackets, it says "company," but in Livno we had the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police, and as I said previously, I don't know whether it has entered in the transcript. Clearly, this letter is being sent via the brigade, so Mr. Andabak could not be given this order directly, and that is why the brigade has been introduced as a kind of transmission. He's probably in the territory of Livno and they cannot reach him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We'll have high-ranking officers who are going to testify as Defence witnesses, we should have General Petkovic and General Praljak, so we will be able to ask very specific technical questions of them. But as far as you know, when this company or the battalion of the Livno military police is under the command of Andabak, normally when that military police unit is subordinated to a brigade, is it not the brigade commander that has authority over that unit? That's what I'm trying to ascertain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if it is resubordinated to the brigade commander, he has competencies over it. But as far as I'm aware of the context, it was not subordinated to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, all right. Then I understand better.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If we're talking about Livno, please tell us if you know. If not, never mind. Do you know whether the military police in Livno, this unit under the command of Mr. Andabak, did it have packet links and could this letter have been addressed directly to them, or did some other way have to be found? If you know, tell us; if not --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never in the Command of the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
