utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of the transcript, let me say that in line -- page 46, line 9, the answer of the witness appears under my name. The answer begins with the words: "Let me just add ...." That is what prompted His Honour Judge Trechsel to intervene, because it looked as if I was speaking, rather than the witness. But I'm sure that the transcript will be corrected in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document, P 05232. It is the situation we discussed yesterday about the police forces and the competencies in dealing with the police forces. So let us move on to the next document, P 03123. It is of the same date, which is explanatory for the previous document. I am referring to document P 03123. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, does it explain the previous document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It explains the one that follows, that comes after it. I think there is a document dated the 20th of September from the Department of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm talking about the 2nd of July. Yes, there's a document after it. Thank you. Can we now look at document 56364 -- 06364. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Will you please tell me whether these activities listed in this document fall within the terms of reference of Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the procurement of material resources from the XY side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Can we now look at the next document, P 02093. It's a document we looked at yesterday, which was shown to you by the Prosecutor. It's an order of the 25th of April, signed both by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Akrap for Mr. Milivoj Petkovic. Shall we look at the document afterwards, P 02089. It is an order sent by Mr. Siljeg, P 02089. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Will you tell me, please, how does Mr. Siljeg see the previous order, and whether this order of his actually relates to the previous one, and what is stated in the heading, can we conclude from this that he is treating the previous order as an order from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he has copied it, he obviously does think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at the next document, P 1205 -- P 01205. Tell me when you find it.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is from the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, in the course of yesterday's testimony, they asked you some questions, specifically Judge Antonetti, "Did you see an order that may have been signed afterwards?" Mr. Stojic, did he ever co-sign an order of this kind? Let us look at the next document, document P 01211. Please look at it first. This previous document is dated the 19th of January, and here we have an order from Mr. Boban, dated the 19th of January. Can you remember, so as to gain some time, it relates to the agreement that Mr. Pasalic referred to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the same date, probably so, and the context is the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In this order, under item 5, it says that the Main Staff is responsible for the implementation of this order. Now will you look at the next document, P 1238. It is the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let's go back to this document, the 1211. I want to make sure I understand what is written. Mr. Mate Boban is giving an order, and he has six items to this order. I'm interested in the sixth item, a request that he received daily reports at 2000 hours. Can we infer from that that he followed, on an hourly basis, the military development in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a rather rare document from which one could conclude that Mr. Boban is interested in the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try to understand, between Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Stojic. I mean, this is a very complex, very difficult question. Under paragraph 5, I can see that he, Mr. Boban, makes the chief of the HVO Main Staff directly responsible for the implementation. How do you analyse paragraph 5? Let me check the translation into English to avoid an -- I'm becoming extremely cautious, and I look at the transcript, which is something I didn't used to do. In this order, does Mr. Boban establish a direct link between himself and the chief of the Main Staff? Does he seem to leave aside Mr. Stojic? What is your opinion on this? Of course, we'll have other witnesses. This is a topic we can revisit later on. But what is your view on this? Because you told us that there are very few documents that directly concern Mr. Boban, and we have one here. So what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, under item 5, Mr. Boban, as president of the HZ-HB and the supreme commander at the same time, he makes the person responsible, when it comes to prohibition of any offensive operations, and he will make responsible the person that he vested his powers on. But I don't believe that this is a re-establishment of a direct contact, irrespective of the fact that we very rarely come upon such documents, and that is a matter of Mr. Boban's personal affinity and interest in the armed forces. And I can tell you personally I never could grasp how he could have functioned in this way, because we practically do not have any evidence on the degree of his interest into these matters. It is, however, part of his purview to do so, and I don't doubt there was constant and -- contacts with the chief of the Main Staff. And, of course, there are other matters which can corroborate this opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I noticed that this is an order dated the 19th of January, which is issued in order to deal with the situation in Gornji Vakuf because there's a conflict there. So this date is this 19th of January, but I'm looking at the number of this order. It's number 23, so that in 20 days, Mr. Boban perhaps issued an order every day, which can show some reduced activity or not, because it seems that his orders are registered. You can see a number, an order number. Were you curious enough, when you did your archive research, to try and see which were the other previous documents prior to the number 23 document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, more or less whenever I could make a photocopy of Mr. Boban's document, I did so, and I have them in a chronological order, but I did not perform an analysis of his actions because that would fall outside the terms of reference for my present report. But your remark is interesting, and in my future research I will take a look at those matters. And that is an issue of supreme command, which is an extremely important matter for an armed force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Yes, Ms. Nozica, you have 25 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at the document 1238. It is at the end of your batch of documents. It is the last document in the batch. It is an order dated the 20th of January, 1993, co-signed by Mr. Milivoj Petkovic and Mr. Arif Pasalic. Let's not complicate matters too much. I would like to ask you whether this is an order co-signed by Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Pasalic and not Mr. Stojic and Mr. Pasalic. And for that purpose, from document P 1205, I would like to read the fifth paragraph, which says: "We would establish and nominate a commission of three out of six members coming from the HVO and the ABiH respectively, which would carry out enablement of the separation order." Could you take a look at this, and has this been regulated in this manner in item 3?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You have item 5 before you on the screen, and in hard copy you have P 1238, item 3. Let us make sure that these are the same.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document, in my opinion, which follows from the document of the 4th Corps, dated 19th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have 25 minutes left, so very briefly, please. The Prosecutor showed you document P 01140, P 01140. This is an order signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic, dated 15th of January, 1993. You were asked by the Prosecutor whether it relies on an HVO order. You confirmed that, and now, Mr. Marijan, I would like to ask you the following: Taking a look at item 1 of this order signed by Mr. Stojic, could it be said, as it is stated in the indictment and has been repeated in the courtroom, that this goes for an ultimatum? Could you please take a look at paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, it says that the Main Staff should immediately establish direct contact with all operation zones and commands of the Army of BiH for the purpose of implementing that order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will continue. So, if it is said in paragraph 1, and you have read it, that the Main Staff should establish direct contact with headquarters and staffs of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then enumerates what should be done, would you characterize it as an ultimatum issued to the Army of BiH if this paragraph stipulates that they should establish direct contact? Briefly, and then we'll go on.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this could be interpreted in different ways, but I do not see it as an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in this case I think we should then not only refer to paragraph 1, but also to paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned colleague from the Prosecution had enough time in his cross-examination, he referred to the preamble exclusively. I did not make an objection, and he will, of course, have other witnesses, and he may lead other paragraphs through them. The next document, P 00933 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, I'm going to ask you a related question which may be sort of secondary, but still seems relevant to me. The date is 15th of January, 1993. This document refers to Provinces 3, 10 -- 3, 8 and 10, because at the time there were negotiations in Geneva. You were on the ground. Did you know that the International Community, together with Mr. Tudjman, with Mr. Izetbegovic, among other people, was trying to set up a political and military system in order to deal with the situation? Were you informed of it all? You see, this is a related question, but I'm seeking to get the feel of what your experience was of how you understood all these events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the 15th of January, 1993. I was at my studies at the time. It was sort of an intermezzo. But at the time, of course, I did watch television, read newspapers. Therefore, I received some basic information about that. What was the situation on the ground and how they understood those developments, that I do not know. I couldn't explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we shall ask somebody else, somebody who was active on the 15th of January, 1993. Very well. Please proceed, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Briefly, could we take a look at document P 00933, please. This is a document co-signed by Mr. Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic. Have you found it, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to -- apart from what you said so far about this document, I would like to refer to item 5. This is also a Christmas greeting to all members of the HVO, isn't it, among other things?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In item 3, does this order include personnel of the Defence Department? Because in conjunction with paragraph 1, 2, it states in paragraph 3 that it also involves personnel of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If it does include personnel of the Defence Department, wouldn't it be logical for it to be co-signed by Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, it could be referred to the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We continue. Madam Alaburic showed you a document P 04 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. I have a question regarding this document. Witness, I see that General Praljak and General Petkovic are mentioned, but I also see that Slobodan Praljak is a higher-ranking officer than General Petkovic, because he's a general-major, that is, Praljak, and Petkovic is a brigadier, so of a lesser rank, so it seems. Is that the way we should understand this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Croatian Army and the HVO had this very strange rank, brigadier, when lieutenant-colonel was eliminated, so it's colonel -- lieutenant-colonel, colonel, brigadier. So in other armies -- colonels were brigadiers in the Croatian Army. I know there are armies where brigadier is a general rank, but in the Croatian Army and the HVO, it was a three-star colonel rank. I think that the ABiH used this rank as for battalion commanders, which would be equal to a major, so this I admit is misleading a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But was Mr. Praljak of a higher rank than Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak is having a higher rank. It's 18th of December. I would like to point your attention to something which was poorly realised, and I believe that Mr. Praljak will speak of it in greater detail. There was an idea of a command -- a joint command of HVO and Army of BiH. There are documents that referred to that, although it was ignored. There was a specific coat of arms, a combination of HVO insignia and Army of BiH. Mr. Jasmin Jaganjac was a co-commander, and Mr. Praljak used to command it for a time, and this is why I believe Mr. Praljak's signature is on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now you're telling us that there was a coat of arms that was specific, where you had the HVO and the BiH that were mixed together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sure that I saw such a thing. It's strange that nobody discussed that here. It was divided by a slanting line, and I'm not sure whether the Croatian coat of arms was on the left-hand side or the right-hand side, and the fleur-de-lys, but I do recall such stamps or documents verified by such a stamp, bearing such a coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Defence will have time enough to find this and to show it to us. Please continue, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the joint command was discussed, and I believe that we showed some of those coats of arms, but we will do so again, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, have you found document P 04145? This has already been shown to you.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We see that Mr. Ivan Bagaric signs this document. I must say that he will be a witness for the Defence of Mr. Stojic, and we will be giving detailed explanation about this and other orders. He addresses this to the Command of Heliodrom Swiz [phoen] and to the commander of Health of the Operation Zone South-East Herzegovina. I refer to that part of cross-examination of Madam Alaburic where she asks you about the direct link between the commander of brigades and sectors within the Defence Department; in other words, direct links with Mr. Stojic. Could you take a look at the following document, please, P 06203. That document explains what a commander of PZ Tomislavgrad about the possibility of Mr. Bagaric having the authority to order him about. First of all, I'm going to ask you whether you've seen this document, and then we will go through it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then I'm going to ask brief you. This is a document authored by Mr. Siljeg to the deputy of the head of Defence Department for the Health Sector. Can we confirm that this was Mr. Bagaric in October?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you confirm or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Bagaric was occupying that position throughout that relevant time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: He explains in this paragraph that he appreciates your efforts regarding your order dated 28th of October, which was not even registered with a protocol number, which concerns the inmates of detention centres, and the previous order refers to inmates, if you recall; isn't it, sir? Please take a look at what it says under item a, the document is not valid, and under B, you do not have the right to command. Mr. Marijan, would it follow very clearly from this document, concerning the attitude of commander of the IZM Prozor, the District of Tomislavgrad, about whether deputy head of department can command or not? I have a host of documents about this.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to add something. I believe that this confusion stems from paragraph 9 about the -- of the decree on the structure of the Defence Department. If it's interpreted without the decree on the armed forces, paragraphs 31 and 32, which governs basic elements of command and control, which say that there is a singularity of command and that commanders are responsible to their superiors and nobody else, otherwise there would be an intrusion of a different line of command, and that would result in dual line of command in the HVO, it would be an absurd situation, because after all, no army can function with two lines of command. I believe that partly what we are looking at can be understood if Article 9 can -- is construed in conjunction with the four paragraphs regulating command and control. Otherwise, this would not make any sense. Of course, commander in this case would be responsible to the operation zone commander, and then the Main Staff, and then to Mr. Boban, as the Commander-in-Chief, if he has delegated his competencies to the chief of the Main Staff. Obviously, he has done so. I should have drawn a diagram to make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We will be looking at the sectors and the commanders, and then I'll show a document which might indicate the chain of command. Now, we leave out a document, and that is 48 -- P 4877. It is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to return to the document P 6203. Unless I'm mistaken, Colonel Siljeg - perhaps he will be appearing here as a witness, I don't know - but, anyhow, it states -- or it's written to the assistant to the head of the Defence Department, so he's writing to the people surrounding Mr. Stojic, to say or to question a given document. He says that the document that was sent beforehand is not valid, that they have no command authority, et cetera. The brigades have to report only through the Military District headquarters. So it's from Colonel Siljeg. This document comes from him. And in military terms, it would seem to be questioning the competence of the Defence Department in certain areas, including, it would seem, in the health area, and that is what is rather surprising. Is the health not part of the remit of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, health was within the competence of the Defence Department, but each unit from the various levels had their own health officials who were accountable to their commander, and they had a professional link with the Health Sector. And in this specific case with respect to the brigade, it would be logical or normal for the chief of the Medical Corps should report to the assistant commander of the operative zone regarding health problems, and then the same report would be sent to the brigade commander so that he should be aware of the communication made. Those were the principles, and perhaps we should look at which document this is referred to. One might conclude that Brigadier Bagaric has directly addressed the brigade commander with something that looks like an order. If he did so, then he overstepped his competencies. But I understand that he's coming so that he can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is precisely what I wanted to ask, the communication between Mr. Bagaric and Mr. Stojic with the unit commander, and here we see clearly that the commander says, "You cannot give me orders."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is it clear -- is this clear from this order?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us go on to the question of IPD, that is, the relationship between the Health Sector, SIS, the Military Police Sector, and IPD. I will cover the next documents very quickly. Look at document 4D 1156. That is the next document. Tell me, is this the unit commander communicating with the Defence Department or the assistant commander for IPD? My colleague asked you whether the Main Staff has IPD, that is, the Department for Morale. We don't have the answer, your answer doesn't appear. What was your previous answer? I see, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I need to answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Who is communicating with whom?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant commander for Information and Psychological Activity with the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The assistant commander and not the commander?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Look at the next document, 2D 1353. I shall have to skip over some documents, and look at item 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. You stressed, with regard to the document of the assistant commander, that it was the assistant commander, not the commander. Mr. Marijan, who would be the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I didn't understand you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Rama Brigade, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Rama Brigade changed commanders very quickly. There was Zelenika, Pavlovic, but I think they came later. I can't remember who it was at that point in time. They had the greatest turnover of brigade commanders, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So 2D 1353. I think you've covered it in your report. Look at item 4: "Communication between the Main Staff." This a report of the Defence Department, item 4, and item 7, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I read it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, please read it so we can see how the communication functioned.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 21st of September, 1992, Main Staff," and item seven says: "With regard to providing information for the public, the Main Staff will forward reports of subordinated command to the Information and Propaganda Department so that it can prepare information for the public."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer, please. The interpreter didn't hear the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You must be a bit slower, and I think that the time used for Judges warning you to be slower must be time to your account, because you try to save time by speaking too fast, then we have to intervene, and that, I think, must be your responsibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is a purely psychological problem. I'm trying to fit in to the time given to me. It's like a 100-metre race and I'm trying to run 200 metres within the same time. So we can leave out the next document. It is also a command to the military police. I don't think we'll go into that. Now, regarding communication and a question that was discussed here, whether the Main Staff had an official of the SIS or not, let us look at document 2D 949.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me when you find it.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report dated the 22nd of November, 1993, and it says: "Pursuant to your order, we hereby submit the following." We see at the end to whom this has been submitted, and under 1 it says: "Names of employees of the SIS who have been appointed to establishment posts, who are satisfactory workers and should be retained in the service." And under 2: "Names of SIS employees who have not been appointed to establishment posts, but who are satisfactory workers and should be retained in the service. A decision must be issued to these workers for the establishment posts they currently hold." Will you please look at page 2, a list of employees in SIS who do not have a letter of employment, and do we see the names of Ivan Bagaric? No, I'm sorry, it's "Bandic" that is written here. Yes, I'm sorry, it says "Bandic." And under number 6: "Predrag Covic, SIS employee, attached to the Main Staff"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have an objection to this question. The fundamental dispute was whether the Main Staff is competent for certain activities in the area of security, but there was no dispute that there was always an SIS employee who controlled the Military Police Administration, the Chief of the Main Staff, and other offices, so I think that was the dispute, and I think this discussion is misleading. The question was not whether someone was under someone else's control, but whether someone has the authority to engage in security affairs that are within the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue. The position expressed has been noted in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... at the transcript and see the discussion between Ms. Alaburic and Mr. Praljak, but let me show one more document, whether the Main Staff has any competencies over the SIS. Let us look at document P 05614, and this would be the answer to the question mentioned now by Mr. Alaburic. 5614.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is not an order. It's a letter to the Administration of SIS, sent by Mr. Milivoj Petkovic on the 4th of October, 1993. Have you had occasion to see this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says that it is necessary for SIS officers to take active participation in resolving and dealing with the following cases of criminal and other activities conducted by certain HVO members, and then we have a list of raping, et cetera. And at the end, it says: "It is your duty to inform us about all mentioned things, results achieved, and measures taken." Do we see, from this document, that there is direct communication of the assistant commander of the Main Staff, Major General Milivoj Petkovic, with the SIS Administration in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this concrete case, yes, we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And I have three more documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to be told how much time I have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] If I may, a technical observation, nothing more. Isn't it logical, if the Main Staff does not have an -- SIS employees for the needs of investigation, for him to address the head of the SIS Administration and the assistant head? Isn't it logical for me to seek assistant because I don't have an SIS official? So is such communication prohibited, what is does this communication remind you of? That's my observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what is your understanding as regards the problem that's just been raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, this can be interpreted in different ways. One way is the one referred to by Mr. Petkovic. What he said is quite logical, though a third question may also be asked: Is this a sign that the Security Service within the units are not doing their work properly? And then the department itself is being addressed, and there's always a problem with documents, as to how to interpret them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may make a comment, I think there is no issue of any blame to Mr. Petkovic in this at all. This is not something that would evaluate whether you did right or wrong. It has nothing to do with it. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, I do not accept that it is anybody's blame, but I'm saying something else. If I don't have an SIS and somebody says I do have it, but from this we see that I do not have an SIS, when Bandic or someone else should have been with me. And I'm addressing the head of the department, the highest level, saying, "I don't have an SIS. You check it out. Somebody has raped somebody, somebody has killed somebody, you check it out." So it's not a question of a communication, that's okay, but the problem is, why should I write to Lucic if I had an SIS employee. Then my own person would do this, Bandic would do this. He is registered somewhere, but we don't know where. He's obviously not with us. So there's no guilt at all that I am raising.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you have six minutes left, but I have a question to put to your expert witness. I listened closely to what General Petkovic has just said. He says that if he does not have a SIS employee, then he has to address the Defence Department. But if we come down to unit level, brigade level, your brigade, for instance, in your brigade did the brigade have -- for the crimes that were committed, did it have military police that could intervene, that could make a report to the brigade commander and refer it to the military prosecutor? Was there not, with the brigade, a security service, the famous SIS, S-I-S, which could also make reports and also refer the matter to the brigade commander? Was that the structure, such as it operated within the brigades of the HVO, or was it not such a structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before answering your question, I would like to add, with respect to General Petkovic, there's nothing incriminating against him here. I'm sorry if this has been construed in this way. As for your question, each unit, battalion, brigade, had to have assistant commander for security. I believe that even earlier we had a problem in labelling them and in establishing lines of reporting, because they grew out of local structures, and in terms of security administration, this was an obstacle to their work that resulted in poor performance in terms of their professionalism. But as per establishment, each battalion and unit larger than a battalion, including brigades, et cetera, could have 15 posts for security officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is where I fail to understand what General Petkovic has just said. If, at brigade level, we've got a deputy in charge of security, then I assume that if we come higher up to the level of the operational zone - take Colonel Siljeg, for instance, or Baskic [as interpreted] - then strictly speaking he should have had a deputy in charge of security. And if we go higher up to the staff level, then, in principle, there should be a deputy in charge of security there. Now, I think that General Petkovic is saying, "I have no deputy," and this is where I'm somewhat at a loss.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the operations level, the zone level, which is a high level, which would be an equivalent to a corps, I must tell you that there were commanders for security, and in the establishment of the Main Staff we used that on the either first or third day. There was, per establishment, no SIS personnel there. Mr. Petkovic has just explained why such a memo would be sent, and this is a confirmation for him that there was no such security service there. But in later documents, we have an SIS officer with an unspecified or unclear position in the Main Staff or there's no establishment order, but what we did have is up to the level of operations zone, the HVO had a structure of officers in armed forces, and the highest structure was this administration which was part of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are going down the same track at General Petkovic and saying that according to the documents you've seen at the level of the Chief of Staff, there was nobody in charge of security, but you are saying that nonetheless there was an officer who did this; is that what you're getting at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me make it clear. Per establishment, establishment determines a single unity of command and it enumerates the posts or personnel that a certain unit or a command should have. I know only of the establishment dated 1992. I have not seen any others, and I'm not sure whether they exist. And in that establishment, there are no SIS personnel in the Main Staff. We have two documents, one we saw recently dated 22nd of November, 1993, which discusses the fact that there are two officers at the Main Staff, and I believe that this is the issue which I think Mr. Bandic is going to testify here, so -- as far as I could gather, so he would be the person to clarify this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have the opportunity to come back to this later. I don't think there's any point in using up your remaining six minutes. Let me just say that in the document 5614, I note that a soldier of the HV -- of the HV has died in Um [phoen]. That's what it says. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to apologise to Mr. Petkovic, if he misconstrued what the witness was asked about. I do believe we have the transcript, the cross-examination by Madam Alaburic on Thursday. We have the transcript of the words of Madam Alaburic, what is disputed, what is beyond dispute. We recall the cross-examination, where the thesis was supported if there was no Medical Corps at the Main Staff, then the brigade commander would directly communicate with the Defence Department representatives. We drew maps and diagrams. The same was valid and said about the IPD and about the SIS. What I wanted to demonstrate is, on the basis of this document, there were two bodies, and what I wanted to demonstrate, and which is utterly logical and said by both Judge Trechsel and Mr. Petkovic, that it would be only logical for him to communicate with SIS personnel and SIS Administration, because for whom would they collect information if not for the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to intervene and to put it on the record, I believe that this is mis-interpreted, my thesis. My colleague, on the previous page, at lines 18 and 19, stated that I think that because at the Main Staff there were no departments or personnels for Medical Corps, IPD, et cetera, that there was direct communication between the Defence Department with the armed forces. This is not correct. My thesis is based on the structure of the Defence Department, on the thesis of the expert witness between different connections with heads of sectors within the department and on the decree that we discussed already.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, fortunately we have the transcript at our disposal, in terms of IPD, asked about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you want to make another contribution, fine, Mr. Praljak, but if it's just to comment on what has been said, that's of no use. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not wish to make comments. I wish to assist. Quoting the counsel, SIS is supposed to collect information and help the Main Staff. This is testimony. SIS does not do so. Military Intelligence Service is supposed to do so. SIS did something else, and it should be left to the witness to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I thoroughly agree, Your Honour. I think counsel has to be careful not to be testifying. That is not the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, nor should other counsel and nor should the accused, I would suggest. I think I had no microphone. I was just suggesting that counsel ought not -- other counsel ought not to testify, either, and the accused also ought not to testify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There is really no need for me to be warned. The Bench is here, and if other counsel have objections to my questions, so be it, but they shouldn't lecture me on how I'm about to do my work. There's the Bench to do so. So I gather that I still have six minutes left for my questions. I have an important question to raise. After this question, I'm going to ask the final question concerning all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: First of all, please take a look at the document, and after that we are going to skip four or five documents, and the document in question is 5188, so P 5188. P 5188. Please notify me when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please tell me first whether you've ever seen this document.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, could you tell me about the line of command that you discussed in your report? And I'll remind you that you said that head of the Defence Department was outside of that chain of command and you've never seen this document, but tell me, with regards to the preamble of this order, who it was addressed to, and is this an example of a single line of command at the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is addressed to all operative zones. Obviously, it would be then relayed to all the subordinated units, all the units subordinated to the Main Staff, and the chief of the military police, most probably to him because of combat activities of the units within the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you read out the preamble to see the basis for this order?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the order from the president of the HZ-HB..."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is drafted pursuant to the order from the president of the HZ-HB, now HR, Republic of HB, Mr. Mate Boban. It is most probably an explanation for its implementation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But it is not attached -- I don't want to testify, although that order has been adduced as an exhibit, but what I wanted to ask you is whether this order demonstrates the chain of command within the HVO the way that you explained it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, finally, I would like to refer to another document shown to you by the Prosecutor concerning -- a document by Mr. Stojic concerning the funding of the HVO, and finally, basis of all those documents that we've seen, I would like to ask you the following: On the basis of these documents, some of which you saw for the first time, on the basis of the documents shown to you during the cross-examination, on the basis of the documents that you had insights into during preparing your analysis, do you entirely stick by your conclusion that Mr. Bruno Stojic, in his capacity as head of the Defence Department, was outside the chain of command of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stick to my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please take a look at document P 10674. This is a document shown to you by the Prosecution. If possible, I would like to have them on the e-court, ERN 0467-2167. 0467-2167. This is not the page. The document is a compilation of different documents. It is very difficult -- oh, yes, this is it. You remember the second page, the order signed by Mr. Stojic. Here, you referred to which amount from this order you made reference to, so that I avoid giving you any leading statements? Which amount you judged to be a very small amount?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, on the basis of my personal experience, the brigade Petar Kresimir the 4th, while I was there, the municipality funded the brigade, and I concluded that this was a paltry amount, the one mentioned here, in comparison with the Bruno Busic Regiment, which is a professional unit, where you could see how much money the companies received, although the companies were very small. I remember saying what was the establishment of the regiment, but at no point in time did it have more than 400 or 500 people. So this amount is paltry, and I'm unclear as to whether -- why it is being given. But as for the final answer, if we take into account the exchange rate of the Deutschemark or German mark, and if we were to convert that into Euro, then you would get the amount.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is exactly what I wanted to do, Mr. Marijan. And I did not refer to your comparison with other regiments or brigades, but I referred to the question of the Prosecution. Didn't you say, asked by the Prosecutor, that the municipality funded your brigade? Then you said, This is a paltry insignificant amount, and the municipality did fund my brigade during that period, so we will -- let us remember that this amount is 3 million Croatian dinars. And now let's take a look at the following document, P 9255, P 09255, exchange rates, and this will bring my examination to a close. So P 09255. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So in January 1993, could you take a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, this will be your last question, because you've used up the time you had.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This is exactly what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, Witness, take a look in the first list what is the value of the Deutschemark in January. 495, as you said. Then let's hark back to Mr. Stojic's memo from January, and if we divide 3 million Croatian dinars with this exchange rate, could you tell us or shall I -- shall I share with you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the reasons why I studied history is because I was poor in maths.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It was just 6.000 Deutsche marks. Would you agree with me if I were to tell you that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no reason for me not to trust you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Does this confirm what you said, that this was an insignificant amount?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this amount is correct, then this is really insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Everybody in this courtroom could make the same calculation. Thank you, Mr. Marijan. I know that you had some personal and family problems, and you sacrificed yourself a great deal for sticking with us for such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to bring my redirect to a close. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on behalf of my fellow Judges and on my own behalf, I thank you for testifying as a Stojic Defence witness, with your expertise and your testimony related to events that were mentioned over these several few days. Our apologies to your family for keeping you here longer than you thought you would stay, but there was no other way, and I hope that your wife will forgive us. I wish you a good trip back home, and you have our very best wishes for your further endeavours as a historian, digging in archives, which must be very interesting for you. The usher is going to escort you out of the courtroom. We're going to have a 20-minute break. It is 20 to 6.00. We shall resume at 6.00. We shall have a few oral rulings, and then Ms. Alaburic will have the floor. She has something to tell us. And Mr. Khan will then have something to say as well, and Mr. Scott will have the floor by way of response, I suppose. So this is how things are going to unfold in the following hour. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As announced, the Trial Chamber will now issue some oral rulings. First oral ruling, in open session, it is as follows: A request for observations by the Prosecution regarding keeping or withdrawing one of the outstanding motions before the Trial Chamber. On the 13th of October, 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion for the Trial Chamber to postpone cross-examination of Witness Mirko Zelenika because his name had been mentioned in the expert report by Milan Cvikl for the purpose of cross-examination on the said report, awaiting disclosure of possible interviews or communication between the two witnesses concerned. On the 14th of October, 2008, during the hearing of Mirko Zelenika, the Trial Chamber issued an oral ruling by which it decided not to postpone the cross-examination of Witness Zelenika, but to stay its decision as to the request for additional cross-examination by the Prosecution regarding communication between Zelenika and Cvikl for the purpose of drafting the report. Witness Cvikl appeared before the Trial Chamber from the 12th to the 15th of January, 2009, and was cross-examined by the Prosecution, including on possible interviews he may have had with several individuals in order to draft his report. Therefore, the Trial Chamber now requests the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or asks, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- asks the Prosecution whether to date it wishes to maintain its request for the possibility to cross-examine Witness Zelenika on the interviews he might have had with Witness Cvikl. The Trial Chamber would like to hear the Prosecution's response straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and all those in the courtroom. Your Honour, this has not been on any particular agenda, I have to say. I do appreciate and thank the Chamber for recalling it to the courtroom's attention, certainly to my attention. I'd be happy to explore it with Mr. Stringer and the other witnesses most directly involved -- excuse me, other counsel mostly directly involved with these witnesses. If the Chamber will allow, we'll be happy to provide some further response by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mr. Registrar, please, let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be another oral ruling later on. But Ms. Alaburic, you wished to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I think it was discussed between us that with Your Honour's leave, Mr. President, I'll address you on the issue that I raised last night, after my learned friend Mr. Scott has been given an opportunity to respond, as well as any interventions by counsel for the other co-accused. And that discreet issue has been dealt with, then my learned friend will take the floor and raise the issue that she alerted Your Honours to. Your Honour, I wonder if that is agreeable to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is agreeable. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to take ten minutes or so hopefully to knock on the head, once and for all, what I described yesterday as the rather lamentable conduct of the Prosecution regarding the issue of summaries. Your Honour, this issue has been litigated and re-litigated seemingly ad nauseam. I always go back to the, if I may say so, very wise and prescient comments of His Honour Judge Prandler before the Defence case started, when he referred to 20 percent of court time being eaten up by procedural issues much. In my respectful submission, the conduct of the Prosecution in relation to this issue stands as a startling example of how time is wasted. Your Honours, the Prosecution have, for understandable reasons, perhaps, tried to import into the Rules a requirement which is not there; namely, a requirement of the Defence to take statements. Your Honour, I have in the past touched upon some important differences between the Prosecution and the Defence and that the Rules that the Judges in Plenary have molded -- have been molded with the benefit of very considerable judicial experience. There is, of course, a huge paucity of investigative capacity between -- the Defence suffer from when compared to the richness of resources from the Prosecution, and of course the quality of statement-taking is, in many respects, a direct result of who takes the statement. The Defence, under a legal aid budget, do not have the benefit of Scotland Yard, French-trained, United States expert police officers who adorn the corridors of the Prosecution office. One could expect a great degree of great accuracy from my learned friends from the Prosecution than from a Defence team that are unable to afford such high-qualified individuals to investigate. Your Honours, the Rules, of course, are also a function of the burden of proof. The Prosecution have to take statements under Rule 66(a) and have to disclose statements, because they are making allegations in this case against individuals, all of whom are of previous good character. The burden is upon Mr. Scott and the Prosecutor to prove the case that they bring. Rule 66 and Rule 68 are clear and unequivocal. They are consistently referencing the obligations of the Prosecutor to discharge his burdens of prosecution -- his burden of proof, and they are completely silent on the Defence. The only Rule, Your Honours, and we must always try to be disciplined, in my respectful submission, and look at the constituent agreements that form the basis of your jurisdiction, the Statute and the Rules, as lawyers. The only rule that talks about additional disclosure is Rule 67. It is titled, unsurprisingly for Mr. Scott, "Additional Disclosure," and that makes it clear beyond para-venture that the obligation upon the Defence to provide disclosure is in relation to special defences and alibis. I have said before, Your Honours, and in my submission it cannot be glossed over, that Rule 65 ter is not -- is a case management tool. It was imported, and it's very clear from the Rules, in 1999 as a device to allow Your Honours to best apportion time and to speed matters up. The Prosecution cannot say, with any legitimacy, in my respectful submission, that the trials that took place in 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998, suffered from any defect or unfairness because there was no requirement of the Defence to submit the statements that they now assert are indispensable to a fair hearing. Rule 65 ter clearly, from the language, from the focus, is a case management tool. In the course of that, the Defence are obligated to provide a summary and a time estimate of witnesses to assist Your Honours. Your Honours, let's put this particular instance of Mr. Bozic under the microscope. Mr. Scott, my learned friend, stood up in court last week, and I'll come to it, and very kindly he provided us with a written motion five minutes before he took the floor, and I'm grateful for that, and he made some additional submissions, most of which we have heard before. But, Your Honours, let's look at the history. In March of 2008, the Defence supplied its 65 ter list. If they were as inadequate, as incomplete as my learned friend Mr. Scott would now have Your Honours believe, one would have expected a diligent, very able, and very experienced Prosecutor to alert the Defence that they had been incomplete in the discharge of their responsibilities. Surprising then, Your Honours, the Defence for Mr. Stojic say, surprising that the response to that 65 ter list was complete and utter silence. Nothing in April, in May, in June. The first letter that could possibly be said to refer to this allegation, this complaint of insufficiency, came from the Prosecution on the 1st of October, 2008. But, Your Honour, that did not allege any particular insufficiency, any particular inadequacy in the Defence summaries. Nothing like it. That letter from my learned friend stated that the Prosecution -- it reminded the Defence that it may make similar requests to those that it made in the Prlic Defence case, and it will assess, on a continuing basis, the Stojic Defence summaries and make requests for more adequate summaries as it sees fit. So from October 2008, again, no allegation by the Prosecution that any specific summary is incomplete or inadequate. The 23rd of October of 2008, a letter from the Prosecution discussing the witness calender. Again, a deafening silence from my learned friend, who yawns in the corner, a deafening silence from my learned friend regarding the inadequacy of the 65 ter summary. The 5th of January, 2009, many months after the 65 ter list summary was properly and timelessly filed by the Defence, and in a letter that was sent only to lead counsel, although I was copied on the letterhead but didn't receive, my learned friend stated that they wished more adequate summaries from Slobodan Bozic and Stijepo Buljan [phoen]. Now, Your Honours, on the 19th of January we gave a supplementary statement. We gave a second supplementary statement on the 23rd of January. And when the Prosecution -- and then, of course, on the 24th of January we gave a third and final summary. Your Honours, my learned friend, before your order last week to give a more detailed summary, accepted, and in my submission it was an acceptance borne of good faith, not of obligation, that we would endeavour to give a further summary to the Prosecution, and that we did. But, Your Honour, when one looks at what we gave, in my submission, it completely and utterly accords with the obligations that the Judges of this Tribunal, not just Your Honours in this courtroom, have mandated on the Defence. And, Your Honours, the case law that Mr. Scott continuously asserts as being supportive of his proposition, leaving aside for the moment my argument regarding the context and the Rules and the purpose, simply does not support his proposition. Your Honours will have read the Prosecution motion of the 13th of January. I'm not going to re-litigate that, but continuously my learned friend Mr. Scott refers to authority. Well, what is the authority? Well, Your Honours, he cites, and we've heard in relation to Mr. Karnavas, that an order has been made to make confidential that which should not have been made public, but it could not have escaped the attention of my learned friends for the Prosecution that the authorities that they prainate [phoen] are confidential. They cite the Buzovski [phoen] case, they cite the Mrksic case, and it's very clear in their footnotes that these are confidential decisions. I pause there. Of course, the Defence cannot possibly be expected to comment on case law which is in the hands of the Prosecution and which it is prohibited from seeing by order of this Tribunal. And I digress again. I am, of course -- I am representing Ms. Hartmann, and there is an amicus prosecutor prowling, as it were, the corridors of this Tribunal, and according to that theory, this disclosure in a public filing by the Prosecution of two documents which are confidential, and the citing of the actual substance of the decision, according to the theory of this amicus prosecutor and the Rule 33 complaint put forward by the Registry, is sufficient to sustain a conviction for contempt. Of course, I say that is balderdash in that case, and it would not, of course, support the proposition in this. But, Your Honours, the Defence cannot deal or address case law which it is prohibited from having access to. What it does have access to is the case law that my learned friend Mr. Scott put in of Dragomir Milosevic. Now, Your Honours, it's very easy for parties to paint with a very broad brush and make very grandiose submissions that are without legal foundation and to say, very baldly, that these are the obligations, but, Your Honour, I do invite Your Honours, when you are considering this issue, to look at the case of Dragomir Milosevic that was cited by the Prosecution, and it is completely and utterly off point. In that case, the Judges were very clear that the Defence team had not even filed a biography of the witness, not even a biography of the witness, and the Trial Chamber in that case ordered that the Defence, at a minimum, provide biographical details, such as name and date of birth, and further detail, such as their occupation during the relevant period and their rank. Now, from any perspective, the Defence 65 ter list accorded with that requirement. So, Your Honours, the one case law that we have access to supports the sufficiency of the 65 ter summaries and does not support the Prosecution's no doubt understandable wish to have more and more information. Your Honours, when reviewing, very candidly, whether or not the Prosecution are able to discharge their burden, I have referred previously to the jurisdiction of my learned friend Mr. Scott, and the fact that in many states of the United States, prosecutors like Mr. Scott cross-examine witnesses without even knowing their name in advance and certainly without knowing the precise contours of their examination-in-chief. And I have said before, Your Honours, and with respect and with your leave, I do say it again, it can hardly be seriously argued that there is any diminution in the forensic abilities of my learned friend, Mr. Scott, simply by crossing the Atlantic. But, Your Honours, when one is looking at the ability of the Prosecution to challenge the evidence that we put forward and that any Defence team puts forward, I do ask you to be very much alive to the entire picture. We have said repeatedly, and it is my consistent position on behalf of Mr. Stojic, that one cannot pass the evidence, one cannot dissect it. The Prosecution have the summaries, they have the exhibit list, but that is not all they have, because in this particular case no less a person than Mr. Scott spent five hours with this witness, and in 400 pages asked this witness numerous questions not about a completely different topic, but including about Mr. Stojic. So, Your Honours, to say in those circumstances that the Prosecution is coming in on the cold and wants more and more information is lamentable, it is regrettable, and it is completely and utterly devoid of merit. Your Honours, my learned friend says, and has said in court and has said in written submissions, that once again the Defence are blaming the victims. Well, Your Honours, I'm not blaming any victim, I'm blaming the Prosecution. I'm blaming them very squarely, because they're wanting more and more. Now, Your Honours, if they were in the position of Oliver Twist and they would come and say, "We want more, please, sir," of course one would try to accommodate them, but in this courtroom, Your Honours, they play the part of Mr. Bumble, lavished with the resources and the abilities that, as an organ of the Court, they are provided with. We, on this side, play the sorry part of Oliver Twist, and so, Your Honours, it really doesn't stand up to close scrutiny, what the Prosecution are asking for of the. Your Honours, the fact that the Prosecution had said nothing at all in relation to the sufficiency of our summaries between March and January, in my submission, is not without legal effect. We had, as a Defence team, a legitimate expectation, given their silence between March 2008 and January 2009, that what we gave was sufficient. They complained in relation to Mr. Prlic's statements. They complained in relation to Mr. Praljak's statements, if I remember rightly. The fact that they were silent in relation to Mr. Stojic's summaries has legal effect. It either amounts to a waiver or it gave rise to a legitimate expectation on the part of the Defence. But to now, with a very small team, in the midst of a Defence case, without the resources that my friend has, to start asking, on a witness-by-witness basis for more detail, has the effect, and I'm sure it's not intended, but it has the affect to amount to an ambush or an attempt to torpedo an overworked and perhaps too small Defence team. They could have done things in proper time. Your Honours, they refer also in their motion to the Krstic case, and, Your Honours, firstly it's very clear that Judge Rodrigues, who is cited there, and it's page 5924, was not making a legal finding. He was simply discussing possibilities, but it's not a legal finding. Again, Your Honours, when one hears a legal submission, it's very important, it's very basic, to go to the constituent document. Judge Rodrigues was not making a legal finding, he was giving an obiter comment. But, Your Honours, when did the Prosecution raise it? They raised it not on the eve of testimony. They did not raise it way after they should have. They raised it at the pre-Defence conference. That was the time the Prosecution should have raised this issue if there was any merit in their submissions. They did not, in that conference, point to particular deficiencies in relation to Mr. Stojic's summaries. In those circumstances, Your Honour, it is our respectful submission that Mr. Scott should not be allowed, as he has said in court, to stand up again and again. I don't need to go into the issues of the applicability or not of issue estoppel or res judicata, but there is a time and place for everything. And, Your Honours, I would ask that all parties, including the Defence, of course, be told to be sufficiently constrained and not to re-litigate issues ad nauseam. Your Honours, a time has come, in my respectful submission, instead of raising the temperature in the courtroom and adding to tensions, to put an end to it and to direct that the Prosecution now should not be allowed to raise further issues on the sufficiency of Defence summaries. That is not to say that we will not in good faith, ourselves, voluntarily seek to supplement when we can. We will. As more information comes to light, we will. But in relation to the Prosecution's right to object and say, "Well, we're going to object to this witness coming at all, we're going to ask this witness's testimony to be put back," it amounts to unwarranted use of prosecutorial discretion, and I would ask Your Honours not to allow it anymore. Your Honour, that's my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Khan. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At this late hour of the day, Your Honour, there's really probably even a one-word response that would suffice, and that word would be "poppycock." I've never heard such outlandish submissions, or rarely have heard such outlandish submissions from such an experienced counsel. In fact, I was hoping this afternoon that -- frankly, I was hoping and indeed even praying, that Mr. Khan might reconsider his course and not waste the Chamber's time with raising an issue which, as he says, has been raised again and again by all Defence, and in fact, raised exactly by Mr. Karnavas some months ago. Exactly. We can't afford to comply with the rules, exactly that argument, which the Chamber, in particular Judge Trechsel, completely rejected out of hand. The Chamber may be familiar with the saying that imitation is the highest form of flattery, and in this regard I suggest that Mr. Khan is flattering Mr. Karnavas by imitating him and putting into practice the notion that offence is the best defence. The courtroom will recall that on the 4th of September, 2008, His Honour Judge Trechsel had these words for Mr. Karnavas, when Mr. Karnavas made exactly these same arguments concerning the adequacy of the Prlic witness summaries: Your Honour Judge Trechsel stated: "Mr. Karnavas, you're talking along the motto that attack is the best defence." So my congratulations to Mr. Karnavas for the compliment paid to him by Mr. Khan in imitating Mr. Karnavas. What is lamentable, Your Honours, what is lamentable, is that we wasted the time this afternoon on an issue indeed that this Chamber has been clear on and has ruled repeatedly on. And it is not the Prosecution but the Defence who repeatedly raises the same question over and over and over again, which this Chamber has repeatedly rejected. Now, let me again briefly review the facts. The Defence is clearly on notice by the Tribunal law and Rules, which are clear. This has been dealt with by pleading after pleading, order after order, which I don't think have been kept secret from Mr. Khan. It's been -- if he's been in court, unless he's not been listening, he will have seen the law, he will have heard the discussions. As far as I can tell, he was here during most days of the Prlic proceedings where all these issues were discussed repeatedly, and it's unseemly for Mr. Khan just to get up and say, "We weren't aware of this law, it's confidential." That's utter, utter nonsense, Your Honour. The Defence have been clearly on notice of what the law requires. Each of the counsel here are experienced, competent counsel. They can read the Rules. Rule 65 ter, it's quite clear. The Trial Chamber's orders are quite clear. The Trial Chamber's pre-Defence order was quite clear. There is nothing -- nothing unclear about this, and I couldn't disagree with Mr. Khan more on his statement of the Tribunal law on this topic. As I said last week, indeed, and I think many of us would agree, there are a number of topics in the Tribunal jurisprudence that are not entirely clear and there's room for debate. This is not one of them. The jurisprudence is absolutely consistent and clear, as this Trial Chamber has ruled repeated -- ruled and applied repeatedly, including at the 21st of April, one of the pre-Defence conferences, in which the Prosecution did raise -- did raise and has raised ever since, at every opportunity at every appropriate moment, the inadequacy of the summaries; first, obviously, in the Prlic Defence case, which it was the first Defence case, but also more generally. We've made the point over and over again. So, again, for Mr. Khan to suggest the Prosecution has somehow sat silent on its hands, I think most in the courtroom would be shocked to hear that, because we are rarely to -- rarely silent about much of anything, Mr. President. Your Honour, President Antonetti, you were very clear. You said repeatedly and specifically on the 21st of April at a conference that the Defence summary -- many of the Defence summaries across the board, all six accused, many of the Defence summaries were inadequate, and specifically citing by example the Praljak summaries. It's on the record. Anyone can get the transcript. It was clearly put out. Now, is it my fault if, in the intervening time, if the Praljak Defence, for example, doesn't take your direction on board, Judge Antonetti, and correct those problems, does it become it's my fault? It's the Prosecution's fault, because we haven't raised it every day? Their obligation is to the Rules and to the Judges to comply, and whether I raise it every day or not, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, your direction, your findings in April 2008, are still in effect and still apply. And until the defence comply with your order, there is not compliance. Judge Trechsel, on the 13th of October, 2008, engaged in a quite clear tutorial, and the transcript goes on for some length at what's required. Unless Mr. Khan wasn't present or didn't have access to the transcript, he would have been clearly advised of what Rule 65 ter requires. He may want to dust off that part of the transcript and review it, the 13th of October, 2008. Judge Prandler, not to be left out, Your Honour, has also raised on numerous occasions what the law requires, and specifically on the 24th of September, 2008, urged the Defence -- urged the Defence, saying this was, quote, "a kind of lesson" for everyone to provide fully adequate summaries "as punctually as possible." Each of Your Honours has clearly repeatedly indicated what the law requires, and Mr. Khan couldn't be more wrong. Now, we did specifically alert them in general, and if Mr. Khan, again, was not asleep during the Prlic case, he knows the position that the Prosecution took during the Prlic case on a number of summaries that were complained about, and a number of times -- and there were a number instances where the Trial Chamber ruled that there were indeed inadequate summaries. I assume Mr. Khan was paying attention. We sent letters on the 1st of October, 2008, and again on the 23rd of October, 2008, raising as a general matter, contrary to sitting silent, saying, "We're still concerned about the summaries. We're going to write just to put you on the notice, if the summaries aren't adequate, we'll raise them as we go." Hardly a surprise, hardly a surprise. I'm not going to go through, Your Honour, because of the hour, I'm not going to go through all the exchange of correspondence from the 23rd of October to date. Let me just jump to the end of last week, when, in fact and, indeed, to make the point, in this instance the Trial Chamber granted the Prosecution motion and did find the summary inadequate. That's not Ken Scott's finding. That's your finding, Judges. You found it was inadequate, and so ruled. And then you ordered -- then you ordered the Stojic Defence to provide a completely adequate summary by the next day. Well, unfortunately, they didn't do that. They provided a summary that, frankly, was no improvement at all, unfortunately. We received on the summary -- and let me give you some examples. One of the topics that we complained about before was the evidence about detention camps. The summary simply repeated exactly the same words. Is that an improvement? Mr. Stojic's de jure and de facto powers, the summary is slightly rephrased, using a few different words, providing no additional information. Number 3, the events that Mr. Bozic supposedly witnessed with regard to Stojic, no new information provided. Number 4, document P 02056 added nothing beyond saying that the witness "will testify to the veracity of documents provided by him and will describe how these documents were created." Nothing more specific than that, and I will come back to that particular item in a few moments. I cannot see, Your Honour, how any of these objections were unreasonable or unfair on behalf of the Prosecution in the wake of this Trial Chamber's filing that the existing adequate summary was not adequate. In response, the Stojic Defence, by way of a letter on Saturday the 24th - and now let me remind you, this is the Saturday before the witness is supposed to start on Monday - finally we get the fourth summary, the fourth summary, and just then there is some improvement. But what's troubling about the fourth summary and which kind tells the tale, unfortunately, is it becomes clear that the withholding of information has been tactical. Let me take one example. I'm going to take one example, I'm going to walk the Chamber through it. That concerns, in fact, this Exhibit P 02056. Concerning that --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I apologise, colleague Scott, I object. The witness is supposed to come into the courtroom tomorrow, and I really think that what has been said about his testimony, especially as we are in open session, should not be presented now. Let Mr. Scott try and -- I beg your pardon. We're talking about summaries, and I think the witness is due to come, and I have a lot of difficulty in understanding this whole story, because the witness can -- regardless of what we put in the summary, he may say something quite different here in the courtroom, once he takes his oath. This hypothetically may occur, Judge Trechsel. I can tell you what he told me in the proofing, but once he takes his oath, he may say something quite different. So I really think that what has been said in the summary and what has been disclosed to the parties should not be went into now. If Mr. Scott feels it's inadequate, though we haven't been told anything to that effect since Saturday, then we will consider providing additional information about -- including about the document he wishes to mention now. Mr. Scott said that he received that information on Saturday. It was clear that the witness could not begin his testimony on Monday, because we had another witness, an expert witness, and it is quite clear that he had quite sufficient time to prepare on the basis of additional information. I must say that all of this is very tiring, and I must tell you, with all sincerity, it's very difficult to work with the witness, to proof him, to talk with him, and to work with him constantly under all these pressures. Yes, my colleague is suggesting to me that the colleague told us that the information we provided was sufficient. Mr. Scott obviously wishes to go further because he feels that even the information provided on Saturday was not adequate. If a specific case is being referred to, I feel we should refrain from mentioning them and from them going into the transcript, which could be harmful for the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's unseemly for counsel to object to an argument that they have put in motion. They've raised the issue. I'm responding to it. And I did not interrupt Mr. Khan as much as I might have wanted to, and I would appreciate the same courtesy. The point was not to ask for more information -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, just very quickly two points. The Trial Chamber was informed that you were satisfied with the information provided to you by the Stojic Defence, so for us that settled the matter. Secondly, the witness is scheduled to testify tomorrow. I think it might be better not to go to the merits of his testimony with exhibits, you know, because this is an open session, and might you want to us to move to private session to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it would assist, I'd be happy to go into private session, but I don't think it's necessary. But if it will assist the Chamber to move this more efficiently, I'll be happy to. I see no reason to whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
