utterances.text: Your Honour, of course it's for my learned friend Mr. Scott to decide how he responds. I didn't once go into the substance of the witness's testimony. My point was the procedural one, the legitimacy of the Prosecution to keep asking for additional information. Your Honour, my learned friend perhaps can be allowed to complete his submissions. I will say, before I sit down, I did make a mistake. In relation to this particular witness, he didn't speak to him for five hours, he spoke to him for five days. So, I'm sorry, that's my mistake; five days, 400 pages, Mr. Scott with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Khan, and your lead counsel has just told us that the witness may say something quite different now, and that's exactly what the other side is entitled to know. It may be something different than what he told sometime ago. But I think, Mr. Khan, this Chamber rather recently has made a decision which is quite clear and which basically accepts the points made by the Prosecution, and you are, it seems, asking the Chamber now to turn back 180 degrees and even kick in the other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will just -- with your leave -- in fact, I think Your Honour, with the greatest respect, has not got the point; not got the point, no. The point of my learned friend, Ms. Nozica, is even if a full statement has been taken, of course there is a possibility that a witness in the dock, under oath, will say something different. That is completely a different issue. Your Honours, that is completely, in my submission -- Your Honour can say no, but in my submission that's a completely different issue. It is well known to anybody experienced in the courtroom that a witness can go hostile. That happens. It happens to Prosecution witnesses, it can happen to Defence witnesses. It's when they come and say something that was not contemplated when they took the statement, and in many cases if the party calling them had known they were going to go hostile, that witness would not have been called. So the point of Ms. Nozica, in my respectful submission, has not been well understood by Your Honour Judge Trechsel, if it's being taken as an acceptance that we know the witness will say something different, not a bit of it, not a bit of it. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I didn't say that. It's not really something to go further into. I understood Ms. Nozica's point, but I was pointing to it that there is also another side to the same argument. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just one final point. I'm not seeking to revisit all the issues. We have given additional summaries for Mr. Bozic. It was before your order, before Your Honours' order, we already expressed a willingness to provide that which we were later on ordered to give. It was not for any wont of willingness on the part of the Defence. We have given a statement in relation to Mr. Buljon, a further supplement. But my point, Your Honours, is that we did see it, in the Prlic case, a proclivity to keep, on a witness-by-witness basis, when there's a thousand and one things for a small Defence team to do, to ask for better particulars. And, Your Honour, the point still remains: Why did the Prosecution, between March 2008 and January 2009 -- and let my learned friend refer to a transcript where he said that a particular Stojic summary was deficient. I challenge him to do that. In my respectful submission, and our junior -- my legal assistant is at the back and has looked at all the correspondence. We couldn't find any instance where any member, not just Mr. Scott, any member of the very able Prosecution team said this statement, this summary is deficient and inadequate and we want more information. The Rules are there for a purpose; I agree. The Defence have to comply; I agree. But there is a time and place for everything, and the time was prior to the Defence case starting, and that has not been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott has to finish. You have five more minutes to complete your arguments, because it's nearly 7.00 and we'll have to finish for the day. Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will only take one minute. I join everything that was said by Mr. Khan regarding summaries, but I would say that what Colleague Scott said is not correct regarding His Honour Judge Antonetti, that at the session of the 21st of April, 2008, he objected to the summaries of all the Defence counsels. I think that His Honour, the President, remembers that, but judging by the transcript, on pages 27376, 27377, and 27378, it can clearly be seen, what His Honour Judge Antonetti said, addressing individually each of the Defence counsels, and he had objections regarding the summaries of Mr. Praljak's Defence. I will not go into the correspondence between the Stojic Defence counsel and Mr. Scott, but this is what the transcript shows. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have to stop. I don't understand why this procedural issue is taking -- is getting out of proportion. We'll have to put an end to this discussion. Tomorrow, we have a witness who's scheduled. I think there was a minor problem because of his eyesight, but I think that's going to be settled. Ms. Nozica, whilst I was listening to you earlier on, I was looking at the schedule. Initially, there were six days that were scheduled. We're already lagging behind by two days, Monday and Tuesday. Obviously, Mr. Bozic is going to continue on Wednesday, the 4th, and Thursday, the 5th, so you might want not to call Stijepo Buljan, who was scheduled for two hours too early, because if he arrives whilst Bozic is not finished, you're going to run into difficulty. So it's up to you. But if you really need the time, because for five hours, you really need six days, you might have to postpone Buljan. I just wanted to flag that out for you. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, in view of the fact that we have another five minutes left for our work this evening, may I have your permission to present an oral suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a minor technical intervention. I think that the transcript should show that Mr. Scott left the court. It must be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, do you need to have Prosecution representatives in the courtroom for what you're going to say? If not, you can speak. But if you need their presence, you'd better say what you want to say another day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just going to suggest the same thing. Tomorrow, at the beginning of the hearing, I would make this oral proposal, and I would certainly wish representatives of the Prosecution to be present. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is 7.00 or nearly. I thought we would finish earlier. I wish everybody a good evening. We shall reconvene tomorrow in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
